mcqs.question: What two checks does the answer skeleton apply to a candidate sharding key, in order?
options: Whether it's alphabetically sortable, then whether it fits in a 64-bit integer
Whether the team has used it before, then whether it matches a competitor's known architecture
Whether it's the primary key already, then whether it requires the fewest code changes
Whether it keeps the dominant query within one shard, then whether it risks skew from a single value
mcqs.explanation: The skeleton checks the dominant-query fit first, then skew risk for that same key — a key can pass one and fail the other. Familiarity, alphabetic order, or minimal code change aren't part of the evaluation the question is testing.

mcqs.question: In the chat-app example, why does sharding by user ID turn "fetch all messages in this group chat" into a scatter-gather query?
options: Because user IDs are stored as strings instead of integers, which slows every lookup
Because group chats are not allowed in systems sharded by user ID
Because each participant's messages can land on a different shard depending on their own user ID's hash
Because scatter-gather queries are required by definition whenever more than one shard exists
mcqs.explanation: Participants hash to different shards under a user-ID key, so a group's messages get scattered across whichever shards its members land on, forcing a multi-shard query and merge. Sharding isn't inherently scatter-gather — a key matching the query, like conversation ID, avoids it.

mcqs.question: What is the trade-off to name explicitly when picking conversation ID as the sharding key for a chat app?
options: It optimizes for 'fetch this chat's messages' while making 'fetch all chats a user is in' worse, since that query now spans shards
It has literally no downside for any query pattern the product might ever add
It only works for chat applications and cannot be applied to any other domain
It removes the need for any secondary indexes for the lifetime of the system
mcqs.explanation: Every sharding key is a bet on the dominant query, and conversation ID trades away efficiency on a 'per-user' query in exchange for winning the 'per-conversation' one. No key is free of trade-offs, and this one still may need a secondary index for the user-facing query.

mcqs.question: Why does sharding by a monotonically increasing ID or timestamp tend to create a hot last shard?
options: Because timestamps take up more storage per row than random identifiers do
Because every new write's key value is larger than all previous ones, so new inserts keep landing on the same highest-range shard
Because monotonic keys are rejected outright by most sharding middleware
Because it forces every read query to scan every shard regardless of the key used
mcqs.explanation: Since the key only grows, every current write falls into the same top-of-range shard while older shards go quiet — concentrating all new load on one node. It's not a storage-size or read-scan issue; it's a write-distribution issue caused by the key's inherent order.
